question_text: A process you designed is now slowing the team down, though it was the right call when you introduced it. What do you do?
option_a: Retire it yourself and say plainly that it has outlived its purpose.
option_b: Ask the team to propose a replacement before you change anything.
option_c: Keep it until someone raises it formally — it is still doing its job.
option_d: Defend it, since the team has not seen the problems it prevents.

question_text: You are certain a decision is wrong, but you have already argued the case twice and lost. The work starts Monday. What do you do?
option_a: Commit fully and make it work, keeping your concerns to yourself.
option_b: Put your objection in writing once, then commit fully.
option_c: Commit, but do the minimum so the outcome speaks for itself.
option_d: Take it to someone more senior than the person who decided.

question_text: A high performer on your team is quietly making life difficult for two quieter colleagues. Their output is the best you have. What do you do?
option_a: Address it directly with them, accepting you may lose them.
option_b: Restructure the work so they interact less.
option_c: Speak to the two colleagues first about what they want done.
option_d: Wait for a formal complaint before acting on hearsay.

question_text: Halfway through a project you realise your original estimate was badly wrong. Nobody has noticed yet. What do you do?
option_a: Flag it immediately with a revised plan, before anyone asks.
option_b: Work longer hours and try to bring it back on track quietly.
option_c: Raise it at the next scheduled check-in with the rest of the update.
option_d: Wait to see whether it recovers on its own first.

question_text: You inherit a team where the previous lead was well liked but let standards slip. What do you do in your first month?
option_a: Set the new standard immediately and explain why.
option_b: Spend the month listening before changing anything.
option_c: Raise the standard on one visible thing and let it spread.
option_d: Keep things as they are — the team is functioning.

question_text: Two people you rate equally are up for one promotion. One has asked for it repeatedly; the other has not asked at all. What do you do?
option_a: Choose on evidence alone and explain the reasoning to both.
option_b: Favour the one who asked — wanting it is part of being ready.
option_c: Ask the quieter one whether they want it before deciding.
option_d: Delay the decision and look for a second opening.

question_text: A client asks for something you can deliver, but you believe it will not solve their actual problem. What do you do?
option_a: Build what they asked for — it is their call to make.
option_b: Say clearly why you think it is wrong, then build it if they insist.
option_c: Build a small version of your alternative to show them instead.
option_d: Decline until they can explain the reasoning.

question_text: You are handed a deadline you are fairly sure is unachievable, by someone who has already been told twice that it is. What do you do?
option_a: Accept it and start, raising it again only with evidence.
option_b: Give a plan for what is achievable by that date instead.
option_c: Accept it publicly and manage expectations privately.
option_d: Refuse to commit to a date you do not believe.

question_text: Which would you rather be known for?
option_a: Being the person who always delivers what they promised.
option_b: Being the person who takes on what nobody else will.

question_text: A project can have one of these. Which do you choose?
option_a: A team that gets on well and works at a steady pace.
option_b: A team that argues openly and moves faster for it.

question_text: Which mistake would you rather make?
option_a: Trusting someone who turned out not to deserve it.
option_b: Checking work that did not need checking.

question_text: Which costs you more?
option_a: Being asked to change direction after you have committed to a plan.
option_b: Being left to decide without enough information.

question_text: Which is closer to how you work?
option_a: I would rather be corrected early and often.
option_b: I would rather be given room and judged on the result.

question_text: Which describes you better under sustained pressure?
option_a: I get quieter and more methodical.
option_b: I get more vocal and pull people together.

question_text: Which describes you better?
option_a: I would rather fix the cause and miss the deadline.
option_b: I would rather patch it now and fix the cause after.

question_text: Which describes you better?
option_a: I say what I think in the room, even when it is unwelcome.
option_b: I raise difficult things privately, afterwards.

question_text: Which describes you better?
option_a: I am comfortable making a call other people will dislike.
option_b: I want the people affected to have had their say first.

question_text: Rank these from most like you to least like you when a project goes badly wrong.
option_a: Taking responsibility publicly, whoever caused it.
option_b: Working out what broke before saying anything.
option_c: Making sure the team does not lose confidence.
option_d: Changing the plan fast rather than defending the old one.

question_text: Rank these from most like you to least like you.
option_a: Telling someone something they will not want to hear.
option_b: Sticking with a decision when it gets uncomfortable.
option_c: Changing your mind publicly when the evidence shifts.
option_d: Letting someone else take the lead when they are better placed.

question_text: Rank these from most to least important in the people you work with.
option_a: They do what they said they would do.
option_b: They tell you when something is wrong early.
option_c: They keep going when the work stops being interesting.
option_d: They change approach when the first one fails.
